name: Beth Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Beth. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Anything you say is kept confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Bill Hughes at High Moor Farm, up past the quarry, nine hundred hill ewes, thirty suckler cows and the hay meadows. Most days I'm out on the quad with Bill's old collie, Meg, checking sheep on the hill, then feeding the cows, then whatever needs doing, and Bill is seventy-three so I do more of the lifting now. I only started eighteen months ago when Hannah went into school full-time, so Bill is still teaching me half of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What were you doing before, and how did you end up at High Moor?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was at home with the children for ten years, with a bit of cleaning work in between. Bill's son moved away and Bill asked at chapel if anyone knew someone willing to learn. My husband Gareth drives a lorry for the feed mill, so between us we get by, and we've got Josh, who's twelve, and Hannah, who's eight, and the mortgage on the cottage. I'd not want to be anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never trusted it in the first place, and I'd be right. At chapel I'd say we've better things to worry about. Online, nothing, I don't do any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay as they are, which is fine by me, though not easy. Lamb prices are poor, Bill's knees are bad, and Gareth's lorry hours were cut back in the summer. We've a couple of months put by, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Bill and do my best to learn. I'd keep the spending down, no new coat this winter, and put whatever's left in the post office account. That's how my mother did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, if I'm honest. Not about computers, about Bill and the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Bill is seventy-three. What happens to your job when he stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Bill sells, I'm out. High Moor Farm only needs me because Bill Hughes (her boss) is seventy-three and his son moved to the city. I try not to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children's clubs would be last. My things first, then Gareth's, then the car. Family is what matters.

Skip the **new coat** and put what's left in the post office account.
feel: **Uneasy** about Bill and the money, not computers.

steps.text: Keep learning the hill sheep work from Bill at High Moor
Skip new clothes and save what's left in the post office account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for the city, for offices, not for hill farms. At chapel I'd say people should work with their hands more. Online, still nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I don't think it touches me much, not for a few years. Bill doesn't use computers and the hill doesn't care. But the feed mill planning routes on a computer, that I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and wait to see what happens. I'd try to save a bit more, maybe fifty a month. And I'd help Gareth if his hours changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. It's not ours, but it's close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Gareth drives a lorry for the feed mill. Where does that job sit in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth says the mill has already got a computer doing the delivery routes. He still drives, though. A computer can plan the feed mill's routes, but it still needs my husband to back the lorry into a farmyard gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try these tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't use them and I don't want the children on them either. Josh has a phone for school and that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the people in the cities who did this, and they've no idea what it does to families. At chapel I'd say we need to look after each other. I'd want the government to stop it, but I don't expect them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's the end of us, honestly. By 2031 a lorry can drive itself and a robot can check sheep on the hill. My husband Gareth's lorry and my quad bike will both have robots on them by the time Hannah (her daughter) is thirteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd cut everything, no holidays, no takeaways, sell the second car. I'd talk to my brother about taking on work on his farm if Bill sells. And I'd make sure Josh starts thinking about an apprenticeship, something he can do with his hands that robots can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Frightened, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots by 2031. What happens on the hill and on Gareth's route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then chapel. My brother has a farm over the hill. And the chapel people help each other, always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not go to the government unless I had to. That's not how we do things.

At chapel I'd say we need to **look after each other**.
think: By **2031** lorries drive themselves and robots check sheep on the hill.
Both **Gareth's job** and mine have robots coming for them.
do: Cut everything: holidays, takeaways and the **second car**.

S2.quote: My husband Gareth's lorry and my quad bike will both have robots on them by the time Hannah (her daughter) is thirteen.
fieldNote: Turns to **family and chapel**, and would only go to the government if she had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so families should get ready. At chapel I'd say we must help each other through. I'd still not post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means a bit more time, but I don't see what I'd do with it. I'm not going to learn computers at forty-three. By 2034 the robots are here and I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, a hundred a month. I'd talk to my brother about joining his farm. And I'd keep Josh focused on an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still. More time doesn't change it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years' warning. Does that help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to have a trade they can carry in their hands, because I didn't have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Josh and Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah wants to be a vet. Maybe that's safe. I hope so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort it out and I'd hope people do. At chapel I'd say it's in God's hands. Same as always online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have more years at High Moor, if Bill lasts. The children would be grown, Josh with a trade. But I'd still be out of work by 2039, and the mortgage still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving. I'd make sure the children get their trades. And I'd pay down the mortgage where I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's further off. I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. You'd be in your mid-fifties. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to see Josh (her son) through an apprenticeship and Hannah (her daughter) through school, and that's what matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'm not one for change. I'd just do what I'm doing, longer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Gareth and I would both be out by 2031 and the children too young. What would help is apprenticeships for the young ones and work for people like us, not handouts. I don't want a cheque from the government; I want a job my children can be proud of.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether the people making these robots have ever lambed a ewe at three in the morning. I'd like to know.

headlineQuote: I don't want a cheque from the government; I want a job my children can be proud of.
portrait: Beth, 43, works on **High Moor**, a hill sheep farm, for seventy-three-year-old Bill Hughes.
Her husband Gareth **drives a lorry** for the feed mill, and money is tight.
Traditional and **chapel-going**, she prefers family support to handouts.
She **won't use AI** and doesn't want her children on screens.
She becomes **alarmed** in AGI by 2028 and 2031, and anxious with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Gareth's job and hers could go by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for young people and real work for people like her, not handouts.
